clinicalPearls: An Epstein-Barr virus-driven angiocentric and angiodestructive lymphoproliferative disorder that most often involves the lungs, typically with bilateral nodules that may cavitate
Extrapulmonary sites include the skin, central nervous system, kidney, and liver, while the disease characteristically spares lymph nodes and bone marrow
Occurs more frequently in patients with underlying immunodeficiency, whether congenital, iatrogenic, or acquired
The lesion is composed of scattered EBV-infected atypical large B-cells set within an abundant reactive T-cell background, an angiocentric pattern that damages vessel walls
Disease is graded (one to three) according to the number of EBV-positive large B-cells and the extent of necrosis, guiding whether it behaves as a low-grade process or an overt large B-cell lymphoma
Presentation includes cough, dyspnoea, fever, weight loss, and neurological or skin manifestations
Management ranges from immune modulation such as interferon in low-grade disease to combination immunochemotherapy for high-grade lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis reflects an Epstein-Barr virus-driven proliferation of B-cells that occurs when T-cell immune surveillance is deficient. EBV-infected atypical B-cells accumulate and invade the walls of small and medium vessels (angiocentric and angiodestructive growth), producing ischaemic necrosis within affected organs, most prominently the lung. A prominent reactive T-cell infiltrate accompanies the relatively sparse malignant B-cells. The number of EBV-positive B-cells and the degree of necrosis define the histological grade, and higher-grade lesions represent a form of EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma, explaining the spectrum from indolent to aggressive behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary infection with mycobacteria or fungi
Metastatic malignancy with multiple lung nodules
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the lung
additionalInvestigations: Tissue biopsy (often lung) with immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation for EBV-encoded RNA
Grading based on numbers of EBV-positive large B-cells and extent of necrosis
CT of the chest to characterise nodular, often cavitating disease
MRI of the brain when neurological involvement is suspected
Assessment of immune status including HIV testing and immunoglobulins
PET-CT and clonality studies to distinguish low- from high-grade disease
redFlags: Progressive respiratory failure from extensive pulmonary involvement
Central nervous system involvement with neurological deficits
Histological progression to high-grade (grade 3) EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and grade-dependent: low-grade disease may respond to immune-modulating therapy and occasionally regresses with immune restoration, whereas high-grade disease behaves as an aggressive lymphoma requiring immunochemotherapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking pulmonary nodules for infection or granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Undergrading disease and undertreating a lesion that is effectively a large B-cell lymphoma
Failing to identify and address an underlying immunodeficiency
Missing central nervous system involvement that alters management
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Grade-directed therapy, restoring immune surveillance in low-grade disease by reducing iatrogenic immunosuppression and considering interferon-alpha
Rituximab-based immunochemotherapy, such as with a CHOP-like regimen, for high-grade disease behaving as EBV-positive large B-cell lymphoma
Single-agent rituximab as an option in CD20-positive lower-grade disease
Correct or address underlying immunodeficiency, including HIV where present
Directed treatment and imaging surveillance for central nervous system and other extrapulmonary involvement
Serial imaging and repeat biopsy to detect progression or histological transformation
Manage under haemato-oncology with multidisciplinary input
